title: Decrease in pressure with increase in the velocity of a fluid
objective: To observe that the pressure of a flowing fluid falls where its velocity rises.
To measure the pressure difference between a wide section and a narrow throat.
To show that the pressure difference is proportional to the square of the flow rate.

theory.statement: Water flows through a horizontal tube that narrows in the middle. The same volume must pass every cross-section each second, so where the tube is narrow the water must travel faster. A manometer tapped into the throat then stands LOWER than one tapped into the wide section: where the flow is fast, the pressure is low. Most students expect the opposite, and that is exactly why the activity is set.
theory.derivationNote: The equation of continuity says the area times the velocity is the same at every section, because the liquid is incompressible and none is lost. So halving the area doubles the speed. Bernoulli’s theorem is the statement of energy conservation for a streamline flow: along a stream tube the sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is constant. For a horizontal tube the potential term is the same everywhere and drops out, leaving the pressure plus one half the density times the square of the velocity as a constant. Speeding the water up therefore takes energy, and in a horizontal tube the only place that energy can come from is the pressure. Hence the pressure difference is one half the density times the difference of the squares of the two velocities. Because both velocities are proportional to the volume flow rate, the pressure difference is proportional to the SQUARE of the flow rate: doubling the flow quadruples the drop. All of this assumes the flow is streamline. If the Reynolds number at the throat rises above a few thousand the flow becomes turbulent, energy is dissipated in eddies, the manometer reading fluctuates, and the simple analysis no longer holds.
keyEquations: Equation of continuity: area times velocity is the same at every section
Bernoulli, horizontal: pressure plus half the density times the velocity squared is constant
Pressure difference = half the density times the difference of the squares of the velocities
The pressure difference is proportional to the square of the flow rate

apparatus.name: Venturi tube
apparatus.spec: wide bore with an interchangeable narrow throat
apparatus.why: Forces the water to speed up at a known reduction of area

apparatus.name: Vertical manometer tubes
apparatus.spec: tapped into the wide section and the throat
apparatus.why: Compare the pressure at the two sections directly, as a difference in water level

apparatus.name: Constant head tank
apparatus.why: Gives a steady flow; a varying head makes the manometer reading fluctuate

apparatus.name: Measuring cylinder and stopwatch
apparatus.why: Measure the volume flow rate by collecting water for a timed interval

apparatus.name: Millimetre scale behind the manometer
apparatus.why: Reads the difference in level between the two limbs

procedure.text: Set up the Venturi tube horizontally and connect it to the constant head tank.
Let the water flow until the levels in the manometer limbs are steady.
Note which limb stands lower, and relate that to where the water is moving faster.
Measure the volume flow rate by collecting the outflow for a timed interval.
Read the difference in level between the two limbs and record it.
Repeat for at least three different flow rates.
Change the throat for a narrower one and observe the effect at the same flow rate.
Plot the pressure difference against the square of the flow rate and find the slope.

steps: Velocity at each section = flow rate divided by the area of that section
Pressure difference = manometer height times density times g
Plot the pressure difference against the SQUARE of the flow rate
The graph is a straight line through the origin, confirming the square law
The slope, with the two areas, gives the density of the flowing liquid

expectedResult.quantity: Density of the flowing liquid recovered from the slope

secondary.quantity: Pressure drop at 12 cm³/s through the 0.35 cm² throat

expectedResult.statement: The limb tapped into the throat stands lower than the one in the wide section, showing that the pressure falls where the velocity rises. The pressure difference is proportional to the square of the flow rate, and the slope of that line returns the density of water as about 1000 kg per cubic metre, confirming Bernoulli’s theorem.

safety: Water and electricity do not mix: keep the apparatus well away from sockets and mains equipment.
Wipe up spills at once; a wet floor is a slipping hazard.
Secure all tubing connections, since a hose that comes adrift under head soaks the whole bench.
Do not exceed the rated head of the manometer, or the liquid will be blown out of the limb.
sourcesOfError: The flow may not be truly steady if the head is not constant.
At high flow rates the flow becomes turbulent and the manometer reading fluctuates.
Viscous losses along the tube add a pressure drop that Bernoulli’s equation does not account for.
Air bubbles trapped in a manometer limb give a false reading.
The tube may not be exactly horizontal, so a height term enters as well.
The tappings may not be flush with the wall, disturbing the flow they are meant to sample.

viva.question: State the equation of continuity.
viva.expectedConcept: For an incompressible fluid in steady flow, the product of the cross-sectional area and the velocity is the same at every section of the tube. It expresses conservation of mass: the same volume must pass every section each second.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the velocity is the same everywhere.

viva.question: Why does the pressure fall where the tube narrows?
viva.expectedConcept: The water must speed up to get the same volume through a smaller area. Speeding it up requires energy, and in a horizontal tube the only available source is the pressure. So the pressure at the throat is lower, which is Bernoulli’s theorem applied to a horizontal stream tube.
viva.answerLogic: Kinetic energy is gained at the expense of pressure.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting a constriction to squeeze the water and RAISE the pressure.

viva.question: State Bernoulli’s theorem.
viva.expectedConcept: For streamline flow of a non-viscous incompressible fluid, the sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is constant along a streamline. It is the statement of conservation of energy for a flowing fluid.
viva.answerLogic: Pressure plus kinetic plus potential energy per unit volume is constant.
viva.commonMisconception: Omitting the conditions of streamline, non-viscous flow.

viva.question: How does the pressure difference depend on the flow rate?
viva.expectedConcept: It is proportional to the SQUARE of the flow rate, because it depends on the difference of the squares of the velocities and both velocities are proportional to the flow. Doubling the flow therefore quadruples the pressure drop.
viva.answerLogic: Proportional to the square of the flow rate.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting the drop simply to double when the flow doubles.

viva.question: What happens if the throat is the same size as the rest of the tube?
viva.expectedConcept: Nothing at all. With no reduction in area there is no increase in velocity, so by Bernoulli the pressures at the two tappings are equal and the manometer limbs stand level. The effect exists only because the tube narrows.
viva.answerLogic: No constriction means no speed-up and no pressure difference.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting some difference simply because the water is moving.

viva.question: Why must the flow be streamline for this analysis to hold?
viva.expectedConcept: Bernoulli’s theorem in this form assumes energy is conserved along a streamline. In turbulent flow energy is dissipated in eddies and as heat, the reading fluctuates, and the measured drop exceeds the prediction. The Reynolds number tells you which regime you are in.
viva.answerLogic: Turbulence dissipates energy and breaks the assumption.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming Bernoulli always applies to any moving fluid.

viva.question: Give a practical application of this effect.
viva.expectedConcept: The aerofoil, where faster flow over the curved upper surface gives lower pressure and hence lift. Also the carburettor, the filter pump, the spray gun, the Venturi flow meter, and the way a fast train draws nearby objects towards the track.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking it is only a laboratory curiosity.

viva.question: Why is a mercury manometer less suitable here than a water one?
viva.expectedConcept: Mercury is 13.6 times denser, so the same pressure difference moves it only a thirteenth as far. For the small pressure differences in this activity the mercury reading would be a millimetre or two, which wastes the resolution of the scale.
viva.answerLogic: A denser liquid gives a smaller, less readable deflection.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming mercury is always the better manometer liquid.

viva.question: Why must the tube be horizontal?
viva.expectedConcept: So that the potential energy term in Bernoulli’s equation is the same at both tappings and cancels. If one tapping were higher than the other, part of the difference in level would be due to height rather than to velocity, and the two effects could not be separated.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the tube is horizontal only for convenience.

viva.question: A ball is held up in a jet of air. Explain using this effect.
viva.expectedConcept: Air moves fastest where it flows around the sides of the ball, so the pressure there is reduced. If the ball starts to leave the jet, the faster air on the side still in the jet gives a lower pressure there, and the higher pressure outside pushes it back in.
viva.answerLogic: Fast flow gives low pressure, which restores the ball.
viva.commonMisconception: Explaining it purely as the jet pushing the ball upwards.

The square root of the flow rate

duringLab.question: Record the manometer reading at three or more flow rates.
Vary the flow rate between readings.

postLab.question: State the density of water recovered from the slope, in kg per cubic metre.
postLab.feedback: About 1000 kg/m³, which confirms Bernoulli’s theorem describes the data.

postLab.question: The limb tapped into the throat stands LOWER. This shows that:
options: Pressure falls where the velocity rises
Water is denser at the throat
postLab.feedback: That is precisely the Venturi effect, and it is the opposite of what most people expect.

postLab.question: You doubled the flow rate. The pressure difference became:
postLab.feedback: The drop is proportional to the square of the flow rate.
